reverse_outline.summary: What the reader will get from the page: sixteen failure patterns, signs, costs and chapter pointers
Key points: patterns as broken cross-system promises, grouped in four families, linked in chains with origins to fix
Opening example of a lost order at a handoff and the guide's purpose of naming sixteen patterns
Patterns grow from sensible local choices and chain from an origin that needs an owner, not blame
How each entry is structured, which examples are fictional or public, and what follows the entries
Order of the four families and why truth comes first
Warning signs call for confirming evidence rather than conclusions
Phantom Stock: quote about site showing stock the warehouse lacked
Phantom Stock symptoms: stale storefront stock and over-promised store pickup
Phantom Stock cause: channels use delayed copies with several writers
Phantom Stock costs and research showing widespread inventory record inaccuracy
Fictional jacket sell-out where layered sync delays caused large oversell and costs
Store-pickup pilot repeating the stale-stock problem
Public vendor documentation admitting its stock figure lags
Phantom Stock remedy: single stock writer, events, central availability, reconciliation (W1)
Chapters covering inventory, ownership and drift measurement
Schrödinger's Order: quote about three systems disagreeing on status
Order-status symptoms: first-message status, missing ERP update, split shipments without status
Cause: money, shipments and returns need separate states in one record
Costs: order-tracking support contacts and financial errors
Fictional split order showing conflicting statuses and repeated support tickets
Vendor docs showing multiple status families per order
Remedy: single order record with separate sub-states and derived summary (W2)
Chapters on order management, service view and ERP integration
Familiar Stranger: quote doubting whether two customer records are one person
Symptoms: stores blind to online orders, privacy requests spanning many systems
Cause: separate customer tables and unowned matching work
Costs: wasted marketing, poor service, and GDPR response deadlines
Fictional customer split across four systems and the decision to delay loyalty
Vendor deprecating its customer accounts, forcing matches to be rebuilt
Remedy: customer master with one id and matching rules
Chapters on master data, privacy and omnichannel stores
Boomerang: quote about a double refund
Return symptoms: two refunders, early restock, spreadsheet credit notes
Cause: returns span three owners with no defined refund trigger
Costs: high return volumes and fraud make double refunds exploitable; provider warnings
Fictional wave of double refunds from portal and manual console refunds
Fictional over-refunds caused by an unallocated stacked discount
Vendor separating return money from warehouse work and dispositions
Remedy: one return record, disposition as trigger, single keyed refunder, daily match
Chapters on returns, payments and ledger
Price Nobody Can Explain: quote about inconsistent country prices
Pricing symptoms: many price systems, unintended stacking, wrong refund prices
Cause: many price setters and copies, silent import failures, lingering promo settings
Costs: margin, parity sanctions and EU prior-price regulation
Fictional German underpricing from a silently failed import
Fictional Black Friday discount stacking from an unreverted setting
No public incident; regulation mandates price history per SKU and channel
Pricing remedy: owners, dated events and campaigns, history, ordered promotions, reconciliation
Chapters on pricing, promotions and B2B pricing
Spaghetti Junction: quote about many unowned integrations
Symptoms: same fact moved by many paths with no inventory
Cause: each point-to-point connector was the quick fix
Costs: hard incidents and upgrades; survey on integration complexity
Fictional integration inventory showing unowned flows and multiple stock writers
Zalando consolidating interfaces into one catalog portal
Remedy: owned, contracted integration inventory with events and reconciliation (W5)
Chapters on integration styles, ERP flows and ownership
Message in a Bottle: quote disowning delivery responsibility
Symptoms: duplicate records from retries and lost messages
Cause: at-least-once delivery documented by vendors, but integrations assume exactly-once
Costs, with Zalando's event pipeline lagging at peak and being replaced
Fictional throttled order flow causing missed delivery promises
Stripe guidance not to rely on a single landing-page signal for fulfillment
Remedy: idempotency keys, handled-event log, owner fetch, dead letters, reconciliation
Chapters on event consistency, integration styles and payments
Pulled Rug: quote about a missed deprecation notice
Symptoms: calls to retired APIs, partner deductions, unread changelogs
Cause: merchant lacks dependency record, reader and tests
Costs and public API retirement timelines from Amazon and bol
Fictional retired API version leaving marketplace stock stale
Fictional wholesale buyer deductions for mismatched despatch advices
Shopify silently changing a stock state's meaning; its versioning calendar
Remedy: pinned versions, changelog mailbox, partner cards, contract tests
Chapters on API versioning and EDI
First Snowfall: quote about failing only at peak
Symptom: storefront survives but back-end syncs fail
Cause: designs sized for ordinary load; load tests skip integrations
Costs, with Target's 2011 site crashes
Fictional Black Friday volumes where platform held but sync and queue failed
Fictional card-testing attack with no kill switch, pausing payments
Shopify's peak testing scale; merchant connectors remain merchant's job
Remedy: load-test integrations, degrade switches, freeze, runbook
Chapters on peak reliability, peak-day journey and warehouse queue
Giant's Boots: quote copying big-company architecture
Symptoms: small teams running composable or headless setups
Cause: giants' publicity and vendor incentives skip the fit question
Costs, with Segment and Prime Video reversing distributed designs
Fictional merchant declining composable and headless rebuild pitches (W4)
Zalando itself retreating from pushed events
Remedy: size by measured complexity; add capabilities only for measured problems
Chapters on architecture styles, build-buy and scaling stages
Burned Bridge: quote about same-day cutover and shutdown
Symptoms: big-bang migration, old system off, contract-driven date before peak
Cause: big bang seems cheaper and risks looked fine in demos
Costs, with Finish Line reverting to a kept-alive old platform
Fictional seam-by-seam OMS and PIM rollout plan
Target's pre-holiday switch-over as a calendar-driven cutover
Remedy: seam migration, keep old path through a peak, parallel run, rollback, exit design
Chapters on replatforming, strangler pattern and composable case
Forked Platform: quote about customizations blocking upgrade
Symptoms: stale agency edits, checkout scripts, unused apps
Cause: quick customizations and no upgradeability owner
Costs, with Adobe and Shopify end-of-support and customization deadlines
Fictional customized theme but untouched checkout enabling W4
Fictional app sprawl and the app governance rule
No public cost cited; deadlines only mark when forks break
Remedy: owned upgradeability, supported extension points, register, routine upgrades
Chapters on extensibility, storefront and checkout
One Size Fits None: quote about consolidating brands for synergies
Symptoms: forced sharing across unlike brands or unmeasured duplication
Cause: cost-led decisions ignoring operational differences
Costs of oversharing versus overseparating
Fictional storefronts sharing one tenant appropriately
Triggers for review and deferral of group-sharing decision
Zalando and ABOUT YOU sharing infrastructure as a public example
Remedy: decide sharing per capability with quantified benefit
Chapters on tenancy, scaling stages and business models
Lynchpin: quote about single absent EDI expert
Symptoms: undocumented connectors and knowledge in one head
Cause: specialist efficiency and invisible value of exit plans
Costs, with Shopify Logistics sale and Zalando Connected Retail ending
Fictional single-consultant EDI, remaining unowned integrations, undocumented ERP connector
Public cases as dependencies merchants did not control
Remedy: ownership map, owned contracts, backup person, exit cost at purchase
Chapters on ownership, exit pricing and partner cards
Long Fuse: quote about a late-noticed invoicing mandate
Symptoms: mandates learned late, no accessibility audit
Cause: scattered rules with nobody tracking them
Costs and public regulatory dates for e-invoicing, accessibility and PCI
Fictional merchant meeting Belgian e-invoicing via Peppol
Fictional regulatory calendar assigning owners and dates
Belgian mandate's notice period before fines
Remedy: owned regulatory calendar and vendor conformance in procurement
Chapters on regulation, e-invoicing and privacy deadlines
Secret Agent: quote about an unknown actor changing stock
Symptoms: shared admin keys and side writers
Cause: easy, broadly permitted apps, with AI agents arriving the same way
Costs, with the polyfill.io supply-chain compromise
Fictional pre-order app creating phantom reservations
Waypoint's responses: integration ownership and agent readiness
Polyfill.io as unseen checkout code ownership change
Remedy: owned, scoped credentials, approvals, human gate for AI agents
Chapters on app governance, security and agentic commerce
Four scale stages; patterns arise at Growing and hurt at Omnichannel
Fictional merchant's ten incidents mostly traced to Growing-stage designs

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

The intro reader named sixteen patterns in four families, the entry shape (sign, mechanism, cost, remedy, links), then scale stages, chains and three uses, with invented Kestrel & Pine examples and dated public cases, matching the expected answer.
Every outline summary agrees with the controlling idea of the spec paragraph aligned to it; the two opening callouts are recorded as placement, not units.
The outliner marked no unit as holding two ideas.
Each entry unit supports S1/S2 (sign, mechanism, cost, remedy per pattern, family in the table), the stage section supports S3 and the chains section S4; the conclusion applies S4.

Both tables are introduced by a paragraph stating what they show; each public figure, quotation and case is followed by a clause saying what it shows for the pattern (e.g. 'even a vendor's own stock copy lags', 'a signal sent once ... cannot carry the order').

Pattern boundaries are carried by the parallel sub-headings as declared; within entries the bold labels carry elaboration, cause and problem-solution; second cases open with 'also', 'repeats the problem' or a time phrase; section and conclusion openings state their relationship ('The stage table treats each pattern alone. In practice one sets up the next', 'It too starts', 'This one starts with a copied decision', 'The sale this page opened with').

results.draft_locus: How the Patterns Reinforce Each Other ¶6
results.quote: then makes the copies trustworthy (W6, W7)
results.finding: W6 and W7 are used as labels but never said to be anything; every other Waypoint decision is glossed somewhere on the page.
results.corroborated_by: flow-A: item 3, same sentence; flow-B: item 3, same sentence

results.quote: The platform's core or theme has been customized so deeply that it can no longer be upgraded
results.finding: 'Core' and 'theme' carry the Forked Platform's warning sign but are never explained, not even in the pattern's own entry, for a reader new to commerce platforms.

results.quote: Pinned versions and sunset dates per integration
results.finding: The Pulled Rug's remedy rests on 'pinned versions' and 'sunset dates', neither of which is explained for the newcomer audience.

results.quote: a page promises a delivery the warehouse's cut-off cannot meet
results.finding: 'Cut-off' is used in the first key point as one of three illustrating promises and is never explained.

results.quote: A 14-person team, Kestrel & Pine's size, runs a dozen composable vendors (commerce bought as separate services); a €48 million merchant like it builds a headless storefront
results.finding: Both readers first took the sign to describe Kestrel & Pine and had to re-read after 'Avoided' two units later; the prose does not mark the merchant as hypothetical.

results.quote: Kestrel & Pine also had no kill switch, a setting that turns a feature off without a deploy, for guest card payments: on the Card-Testing Night of August 2026, 48,000 bot attempts with stolen cards hit the guest checkout
results.finding: Both readers found an August fraud attack out of place in the peak-load entry; the spec itself declares this unit in The First Snowfall.

results.draft_locus: How the Patterns Reinforce Each Other ¶6
results.quote: then adds the hubs (W2, an OMS for orders; W3, a PIM for product content), then makes the copies trustworthy (W6, W7), and keeps the platform (W4)
results.finding: Both readers had to look back for the Waypoint decisions: W3 is first named here and W6, W7 are never explained, so the repair order reads as unexplained labels.

results.quote: Nine appear above, in the "At Kestrel & Pine" paragraphs; the tenth, the Store Stock Mirage of December 2026 (Utrecht promising sold stock), is the Phantom Stock seen from a store. Black Friday week's stacking bug and order backlog are not among them.
results.finding: Both readers re-read this: the nine are not identifiable, the December pickup case above appears to be the 'tenth' that supposedly does not appear above, the Black Friday exclusions are unexplained, and the supporting stage-map sentence comes last.

results.quote: In the Black Friday week before, a stacked discount (see The Price Nobody Can Explain) left **190** returned jackets refunded at €159.20 instead of the €143.28 actually paid
results.finding: The cause is sent forward to an entry not yet read, so flow-B met the effect unexplained and had to work out the figures; the forward reference follows from the spec's truth-family order and its declared p35a.
results.corroborated_by: flow-A: item 3, same sentence (noted as a small hesitation)

results.quote: the messages arrived, but **four hours** late, and nothing watched their age, so roughly **8,000 orders** missed the next-day delivery the storefront had promised
results.finding: Flow-B re-read to see how a late-under-load case fits a warning sign about duplicates and gaps; the prose does not tie lateness back to the mechanism ('late or never').

results.quote: a signal sent once, from a page the shopper may never reach, cannot carry the order, so fulfillment must also listen for the payment provider's own message.
results.finding: Flow-B had to re-read the Stripe quotation to see how it shows the pattern; the link to 'sent once and trusted' is left indirect.

results.quote: The stock sync chain and the WMS connector queue did not: the oversell, the backlog and the €52,000 stacking bug above.
results.finding: Flow-B was confused that a leftover configuration setting is listed among things that peak load broke, which blurs the First Snowfall's mechanism.
Opens on a puzzling scenario (a sale the warehouse never receives while both systems stay up), not a placeholder or restated question.
The conclusion opens with a synthesis sentence, calls back, gives three uses declared as the takeaway and hands off; no 'in conclusion' opener, grab bag or new subtopic.

'a promise is broken somewhere other than where it was made ... So the remedy is rarely a new platform; it is ownership, contracts and reconciliation' synthesizes the three sections and answers so-what.
'The sale this page opened with now has a name, a Message in a Bottle, and a place to look: upstream, for a connector nobody owns.'
The reader named the Message in a Bottle, integration family, the Spaghetti Junction upstream, and the idempotency key, handled-event record and reconciliation, as expected.
The reader gave all four families with the expected one-clause diagnosis each, from the KEY POINTS.
The reader asked for the integration inventory, owners per flow, reconciliation coverage and the number of writers per fact, as expected; missing thresholds do not block the expected answer.
